ending: The anonymous book of the maids' testimonies, titled simply for the help who told them, is published and read all over Jackson, throwing the town's white households into suspicion and unease. Hilly Holbrook recognizes herself in one of the stories and burns to expose and punish the maids and Skeeter, but she is trapped: to prove the book is about Jackson would be to admit that she is the woman fooled by Minny's notorious secret revenge, the pie she was tricked into eating, and so she is forced into silence. The fallout still lands hard on the women. Aibileen is falsely accused of theft by Hilly and dismissed from the Leefolt house, yet she walks away with a sense of freedom and a possible future as a writer, having found her own voice. Minny, emboldened, finally resolves to leave her abusive husband and holds a secure place with the loyal Celia Foote. Skeeter, shunned by her old circle but offered a publishing job, departs for New York with her family's blessing to pursue her ambitions. Skeeter has also learned the sad truth of what became of Constantine, the maid who raised her. The three narrators part changed, having risked everything to tell the truth.
in_short: In Jackson, Mississippi, in the early 1960s, a young white would-be writer, Skeeter, secretly sets out to record the true experiences of the Black maids who raise white families' children and keep their homes. Aibileen, a wise, grieving maid, cautiously agrees to talk, followed by her sharp-tongued friend Minny and, after the murder of Medgar Evers, many others. The project is dangerous in a town ruled by the segregationist socialite Hilly Holbrook, who champions separate bathrooms for the help. Minny takes a job with Celia Foote, a kind outcast, and holds a secret weapon against Hilly, a humiliating trick she once played on her. Skeeter also uncovers what happened to Constantine, the maid who raised her. The book of the maids' stories is published anonymously and sends shockwaves through Jackson. Hilly, recognizing herself, is silenced by fear of exposure. Aibileen loses her job but steps toward a freer future, Minny gains security, and Skeeter leaves for New York, the three women changed by what they dared to do.

recaps.text: In Jackson, Mississippi, in 1962, Aibileen Clark, a Black maid, works for the anxious young Elizabeth Leefolt, raising the couple's neglected toddler while quietly mourning her own grown son, who died not long before. Aibileen's best friend, Minny Jackson, a superb cook with a defiant streak, has just been fired by the imperious Hilly Holbrook and struggles to find a new position. Meanwhile Eugenia 'Skeeter' Phelan, a white college graduate and aspiring writer, returns home restless and out of step with her marriage-minded friends, and troubled by the unexplained disappearance of Constantine, the maid who raised her. Hilly, the ruthless leader of their social set, pushes a campaign to make white families install separate bathrooms for their Black help, an initiative that unsettles Skeeter and sets her thinking about the gulf between the women she knows and the women who serve them.

Skeeter lands a small newspaper job answering housekeeping questions and turns to Aibileen for the answers, and through their careful conversations an idea takes shape: a book that would tell, honestly, what it is like to be a Black maid working for white families in Mississippi. The notion is perilous for everyone involved, since discovery could cost the maids their jobs, their safety, or their lives. After long hesitation, Aibileen agrees to be interviewed and to help persuade others. Minny, meanwhile, finds work with Celia Foote, a naive, warm-hearted young woman married into money but frozen out by Hilly's circle, who treats Minny with a startling and disarming kindness. As Skeeter begins secretly recording Aibileen's story, the risks mount and the distance grows between Skeeter and the friends whose prejudices she is quietly coming to reject.

The secret project inches forward as Skeeter and Aibileen record more of the maids' experiences, meeting in hiding to avoid discovery. Minny settles into the strange, tender arrangement of working for Celia, whose loneliness and unfitness for Jackson society gradually reveal a genuine, vulnerable friend beneath the awkwardness. Skeeter is drawn into a courtship with Stuart Whitworth, a senator's son, even as her growing double life pulls her away from Hilly and the others. Hilly's petty cruelties sharpen, and the danger of the book presses closer, with only a handful of maids willing to risk speaking. The white and Black worlds of Jackson remain rigidly divided, and Skeeter walks an ever finer line between the society she was raised in and the truth she is helping to set down, aware that exposure would ruin them all.

The murder of the civil rights leader Medgar Evers shakes Jackson's Black community and hardens the stakes of everything Skeeter and the maids are doing. In its wake, and with growing trust, many more maids come forward to add their stories, giving the book the range it needs to have a chance at publication. The work is exhausting and frightening, carried out in stolen hours under constant threat of being found out. Aibileen and Minny help gather and shape the accounts, weighing how much can safely be told. Skeeter's romance with Stuart falters as her secret life and her changing conscience pull her further from the expectations of her mother and her friends. As the manuscript takes form and a New York editor shows cautious interest, the women race to finish while shielding their identities and the identity of the town itself.

At a grand society benefit, the tensions of Jackson boil over in public embarrassment, and the fault lines among the women widen. To protect the maids if the book is ever traced to Jackson, they include a disguised account of the humiliating trick Minny once played on Hilly, calculating that Hilly's dread of being identified as its victim will keep her from ever admitting the book is about their town. As publication nears, the collaborators brace for the consequences. Skeeter finally learns the painful truth about Constantine, the maid who raised her: a cruelty involving Constantine's daughter and Skeeter's own mother that drove Constantine from the household. With the manuscript complete and heading into print, the three women wait, knowing that once it appears, nothing in their lives will be the same.

The book is published anonymously and races through Jackson, as white women anxiously wonder whether they appear in it and which maids might have spoken. Hilly recognizes herself and is enraged, but the buried story of her humiliation traps her: to prove the book is set in Jackson would be to confess to being its victim, so she is forced into a furious silence. The consequences still fall unevenly. Hilly engineers Aibileen's firing on a false accusation, yet Aibileen leaves the Leefolt house with a new sense of freedom and the hope of becoming a writer, having discovered her own voice. Minny, made braver by all that has happened, resolves to leave her abusive husband and holds a secure place beside the devoted Celia. Skeeter, cut off from her old friends but offered a job at a New York publisher, departs to build the life she wants. The three narrators, bound by what they risked together, part changed and unbowed.
